prompt:
Write an essay of about 800 words on the subject below.

Write it the way an excellent, idiosyncratic human essayist would: someone with real expertise and strong opinions, writing in the first person for their own blog. Commit to a specific thesis that a thoughtful reader might disagree with. Use concrete particulars (names, numbers, incidents, things only someone who had done the work would know) in place of general statements. Vary sentence length. No headings, no bullet points, no summary paragraph at the end, and none of the stock phrases of AI writing.

Output only the essay, with no title.

Subject: an essay of advice for a new PhD student on choosing a research problem
raw:
The best advice I ever got about choosing a research problem came from a bored postdoc in the back row of a seminar at Berkeley, delivered as a throwaway line over bad coffee: "Work on something where you know why the question is interesting, not just why the answer would be useful." I've spent nine years since then watching grad students ignore this, and I've come to believe something stronger, something I'll defend even though half my colleagues think it's irresponsible: you should choose the problem that fascinates you irrationally, and you should actively distrust the strategic part of your brain that tells you to pick something "hot."

Here's what usually happens instead. A first-year arrives, reads papers for six months, notices that a particular area has a lot of activity—conferences, special issues, thesense that Important People care—and pivots toward it. This feels like prudence. It's actually outsourcing your taste to a lagging indicator. By the time an area feels hot to a newcomer, the interesting foundational questions in it are typically two or three years gone. What remains is the mopping-up: incremental improvements, benchmarks nudged up by 2%, the scholarly equivalent of franchise films. You will spend four or five years, the years when your energy and plasticity are at their peak and your obligations are at their minimum, doing mopping-up, because you chose based on a queue that was already long when you joined it.

I can name names from my own field, because this pattern is field-independent but the examples are local. My friend Dana—smart, technically stronger than me by any measure—spent her PhD on compressing models after the compression wave had crested. Forty-seven papers on distillation passed through her related-work section. She defended competently and left research entirely, telling me over noodles that she never once had the feeling of "being the only person in the world who cared about this, which was the feeling I actually wanted." Compare that with Marcus, who decided in his second year to study failures of a particular old algorithm on adversarially weird inputs—a topic exactly three people on earth were working on, none of them famous. It wasn't fashionable. It wasn't even well-posed at first; he spent a year failing to state his own question crisply. But the field eventually turned toward robustness, and when it did, he was one of the only people who had already done the boring foundational labor. The lesson people draw from Marcus's story is "get lucky on timing." That's the wrong lesson. The right one is that depth in an unfashionable problem compounds in a way that positioning in a fashionable one cannot, because the fashionable area is crowded with people as smart as you, and the unfashionable one is crowded with the question itself.

Now the caveats, because this advice is genuinely dangerous in a specific way, and you should know how. Your advisor matters. A mediocre advisor in a boring-to-you area will starve you worse than a great advisor in an area you merely tolerate. When I say follow your irrational fascination, I mean among problems where someone competent is willing to guide you—someone who has produced PhD students who are still in the field five years later. Ask for that statistic directly; I did, at my prospective advisor's office, and his slightly offended precision ("four of five are still publishing") told me more than any statement of research vision. Also, your irrational fascination must survive contact with actual grind. Be honest with yourself about the difference between loving an idea and loving to think. I loved the idea of causal inference for about four months in 2016 until I realized I hated deriving identification conditions, at which point my "passion" evaporated with embarrassing speed. Test the fascination before you commit: spend two weeks trying to make one small piece of it work, badly, at night, unpaid. If you find yourself doing it when you don't have to, you've learned something real.

One more heresy while I'm at it: ignore most advice about "important problems." Every field maintains a public list of grand challenges, and I have watched students pick from it like items on a menu, reasoning that a Nobel-adjacent problem at least fails nobly. It doesn't work like that. The big named problems are big precisely because they resist frontal assault, and a thesis is a frontal assault by a first-year. The people who crack them almost always arrived sideways, carrying tools and obsessions developed on something smaller and stranger. Yang and Mills weren't trying to solve the mass gap problem; it's named after them. Your job is to find the thing that is small enough for your hands but strange enough that nobody else's hands are on it. The right size, in my experience, is a question you can state in one sentence to a smart non-expert, whose answer you can partially attack within a year, and whose complete answer would make you slightly furious, in a covetous way, if someone else got there first. That last criterion—covetousness—is the true diagnostic, and nobody puts it in the guidebooks.

Practical mechanics, briefly, because abstractions alone are cruel. Keep a private notebook of every question you find yourself explaining badly in seminars—half of my own thesis came from a question I flubbed answering in week three and stewed about for months. Read papers from fields adjacent to yours deliberately, one a week, looking for tools that don't exist where you are; cheap cross-pollination is the single highest-yield strategy available to a junior researcher precisely because it requires no brilliance. And give yourself a hard deadline—end of second year, absolute latest—for committing to a problem. Extended exploration feels productive and is mostly anxiety management. The students I've seen fail to finish were rarely the ones who picked wrong; they were the ones who never quite picked, defending the search itself.

You will get this wrong in some respect no matter what; I did, twice. But pick wrong for your own reasons, at a scale your hands can hold, and you'll finish with something rarer than a hot paper—an actual mind, yours, developed at depth on a thing nobody assigned you. That's what the degree secretly certifies, and it's why following the crowd to get it defeats the point entirely.
